item.title: investingLive European news wrap: Markets consolidate after the US CPI shock
item.description:
Headlines:

  • Ethereum extends losses after the US CPI as risk sentiment deteriorates further. What's next?
  • Why do altcoins crash so much harder than Bitcoin?
  • Oil remains supported amid persistent Middle East tensions as US weighs using "Mother of All Bombs"
  • Bitcoin sinks after the US CPI as markets get increasingly worried about the growth outlook
  • US inflation worries aren't over yet as PPI and retail sales pose fresh risks for markets
  • Gold whipsaws after US CPI as data falls short of bringing an October rate hike back into play
  • European stock market open: Equities under pressure as Wall Street selloff weighs on sentiment
  • France inflation rises sharply in September as price pressures add to ECB rate hike dilemma
  • Macro pulse: Treasury yields may be falling for now, but borrowing costs are still painfully high
  • What are the main events for today?
  • FX option expiries for 15 October 10am New York cut
  • Chart of the day: Gold rebounds as dollar and yields fall, but $4,200 remains a major hurdle
  • US stocks might have a bigger problem than just hotter inflation

Markets:

  • WTI crude oil up 0.04% to $95.08

  • Gold up 1.22% to $4,154

  • EUR leads, AUD lags

  • S&P 500 down -0.31% to 7,746

  • US 10y Treasury yield down 11 bps to 5.08%

  • Bitcoin down -0.86% to $80,856

It's been another relatively quiet session with no major news or economic data releases. On the economic data front, the highlight of the session was the monthly UK GDP report which beat expectations across the board. The data didn't change much, though, as it just reinforced the expectations for a BoE rate hike in November, which was already priced in. 

We also had BoE's Greene and BoE's Breeden speaking, with the former continuing to push for rate hikes to avoid second-round effect, while the latter pointing to soft labour market conditions as basis for a more patient approach in absence of clear second-round effects. ECB members have also been pointing to lack of second-round effects as a reason to be less aggressive on further tightening. 

On the markets side, crude oil continues to edge higher amid lack of improvements in the Middle East. As a reminder, the Saudi Arabia-Houthis conflict has intensified recently with the Houthis attacking many Saudi targets, including Riyadh's international airport and the Aramco headquarters complex in Dhahran. They have threatened further attacks on airports and energy infrastructure, while Saudi-backed forces are fighting the Houthis inside Yemen.

Commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz continues to be disrupted. Two vessels sank recently after being hit by Iranian forces. Iran's leadership said it will continue fighting until the US accepts its demands.

Finally, Reuters reported today that, according to CNN, the US military has developed contingency plans that could include using the MOAB bomb(the largest non-nuclear bomb) against Iranian energy infrastructure or nuclear-related sites if Trump orders renewed combat operations. Reuters added it could not independently verify the report, and this is just contingency planning, not confirmation that the bomb will be used.

Most other markets have been consolidating after yesterday's US CPI shock. The higher than expected US Core CPI triggered a selloff in risk assets, but the minor changes in rate hike expectations and the dovish repricing further out the curve, suggest the market might be starting to get more concerned about the growth outlook.

It’s interesting that stocks, copper, crypto, the US dollar and yields are all trading lower today, while gold has regained all the losses. It feels more like a stagflationary environment where risk assets and the US dollar generally underperform, while gold outperforms.

Looking ahead, we have the Flash PMIs, the FOMC, the US-Iran negotiations and the US midterm elections as key catalysts. If the economic data starts pointing to deteriorating economic conditions, then we could see the market getting increasingly worried about growth. What could drastically change the outlook would be an end to the US-Iran war, as that would immediately improve the growth outlook.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Ethereum extends losses after the US CPI as risk sentiment deteriorates further. What's next?
item.description:
Ethereum tumbled yesterday following the hotter than expected US Core CPI, with a broader risk-off sentiment in the crypto market adding to the pressure.

The limited changes in rate hike expectations and the dovish repricing further out the curve, though, suggest that markets might be getting increasingly more concerned about the growth outlook.

If these expectations get confirmed by deteriorating economic data, Ethereum could remain under pressure as traders will likely reduce exposure to risk-sensitive assets like cryptocurrencies.

On the positive side, Interactive Brokers launched Ethereum staking for eligible US clients on October 13, broadening access to staking rewards. Meanwhile, Ethereum's Glamsterdam upgrade is progressing through testnet development, focused on increasing network capacity and improving transaction processing. These developments, though, are longer-term and are unlikely to offset the macro-driven negatives in the short term.

Looking ahead, we have the Flash PMIs, the FOMC, US–Iran negotiations and the US midterm elections as potentially strong catalysts. Deteriorating economic data could increase concerns about growth, further weighing on risk sentiment and Ethereum.

What could change the picture completely would be an end to the US–Iran war, as that would ease inflationary pressures, improve the growth outlook and likely support a broader recovery in risk assets, including Ethereum.

 

ETHEREUM TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that Ethereumis trading around the key 2,360 support zone and the major trendline. We can expect the dip-buyers to step in around these levels, with a defined risk below the trendline, to position for a rally into the 3,400 level. The sellers, on the other hand, will need the price to break below the trendline to open the door for new lows and target the 1,900 level next.

ETHEREUM TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, since the price made a new lower low, we now have a downward trendline defining the bearish momentum. If we get a pullback into the downward trendline, we can expect the sellers to lean on it, with a defined risk above it, to keep targeting a break below the major upward trendline. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to increase the bullish bets into new highs, with the 2,570 level as the first target.

ETHEREUM TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, we can see the price broke below the tight box yesterday following the US CPI report and extended the drop as more sellers piled in to target the 2,360 support and the trendline. There’s not much we can add here as the buyers will have a better risk to reward setup around the support and the major upward trendline, while the sellers will need a break below the upward trendline to open the door for new lows. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

Today we get the US PPI, the US Retail Sales and the latest US Jobless Claims figures. We have also Fed Chair Warsh speaking very late in the day in a fireside chat with IMF Managing Director Georgieva. He’s against forward guidance, so he’s unlikely to give any policy signal, but it’s worth keeping an eye on it.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Why do altcoins crash so much harder than Bitcoin?
item.description:
When you look at your screener and notice that Bitcoin is down 5%, you will more often than not also catch that smaller cryptocurrencies are plunging by 10% or even 20%. They are all part of the same crypto market, so it is natural to expect the direction of travel to be the same. But why is the magnitude of the moves so stark?

Well, the important difference is more in how these cryptocurrencies trade.

Just think of an example where you are trying to sell a second-hand Toyota Corolla. It's a fairly popular car, so chances are you'll easily find someone willing to buy it without having to knock too much your asking price.

But now, imagine that you are trying to sell a heavily customised sports car instead. Sure, the car is worth more than the Toyota Corolla and by quite a fair bit for sure. But then, how many people are actually to buy that exact car with such a niche set of specifications? Probably not very many. And if there is a sudden need to sell the car by tomorrow, you might very well have to let it go at a hefty discount in order to find someone that might be interested in buying.

So, how does this tie back to the crypto market?

With Bitcoin, there's generally a much bigger crowd of people looking to buy and sell. So even when investors start selling, there's a better chance of finding someone who would be willing to buy at a price close to the current market value.

As for smaller altcoins, it isn't quite the same story. Just imagine everyone suddenly trying to sell their heavily customised sports cars at the same time, only to realise that there aren't nearly enough interested buyers around. So, what happens next? Sellers will then have to lower their prices to attract buyers and the more desperate they become, the bigger those discounts might get.

And that is essentially what traders mean by liquidity. The easier it is to find a buyer without having to offer a hefty discount, the more liquid the market is.

Then, there's also the concept of market depth. Just imagine trying to sell an altcoin at $10, but there are only so many buyers at that price to purchase a few coins. The next set of buyers might only be willing to pay $9.50, while others are waiting at $9 to get in on the action. So if enough investors are rushing to sell, the price has to keep dropping to find willing buyers.

And if that wasn't bad enough, some traders are also betting on these cryptocurrencies using borrowed money. So when prices fall too drastically, their exchanges may automatically sell their holdings to prevent further losses. That is what we call forced liquidation. And when those automatic sales start piling up, they can push prices even lower and lead to yet another round of selling. In essence, one price drop triggers another and that turns a relatively ordinary selloff into something much more painful.

So the next time you see Bitcoin falling by 5% while your favourite altcoin tumbles by 15%, don't just assume that something terrible has happened to the smaller cryptocurrency. Sometimes, it is just simply a case of too many sellers chasing too few buyers.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: US inflation worries aren't over yet as PPI and retail sales pose fresh risks for markets
item.description:
The hotter-than-expected US CPI report yesterday was already enough to give markets a bit of a headache. And despite the initial surge higher in Treasury yields fading, there's still evidence of jitters with equities staying under pressure today. So if investors are hoping for some breathing room to get by, I'm afraid there might be more bad news to deal with as we're not quite done with the inflation and economic data risks just yet.

Looking to the session ahead, there are three key US economic data releases to watch out for:

  • September PPI: This will be another inflation test, this time looking at price pressures faced by producers
  • September retail sales: This will be a key gauge of consumer spending and whether higher prices are actually slowing demand
  • Weekly initial jobless claims: This will be a timely check on whether the US labour market is starting to show more signs of weakness

Given the backdrop this week, I'd argue that the PPI and retail sales will carry the bigger risks for markets.

A hot PPI reading later will only add to inflation concerns after the stronger consumer price numbers seen yesterday. It could offer an indication that price pressures are proving to be more stubborn than the Fed would like. And if retail sales also surprises to the upside, that could stir up a potentially uncomfortable combination for the Fed to deal with.

I mean, if businesses are facing higher costs while consumers are continuing to spend freely, where exactly is the slowdown that's supposed to help bring inflation under control? On paper, that is the sort of scenario that could put renewed upward pressure on Treasury yields and the dollar, while leaving equities struggling for support - more so than they already are.

Having said that, I still reckon it's a tall order to shift Fed rate hike expectations for October at this stage. After the initial spike in market odds to the inflation numbers yesterday, Fed funds futures are now only pricing in a roughly 29% probability of a rate hike this month. That is not all too much changed from around 22% odds before the September CPI report.

As such, the market reaction to a stronger-than-expected set of numbers from both the PPI and retail sales data could arguably be something similar. It might be enough to produce a jolt upon the initial reaction, but will it be enough to really convince of a move in October? I wouldn't be one to put my money on that.

December, however, is looking almost like a done deal at this stage. So, I would argue that the data trend this week could at best solidify expectations of another move by year-end; just not for October.

The other item on the agenda today is the weekly jobless claims data. A notable rise here could complicate the picture by suggesting that the labour market is weakening even as inflation stays elevated.

So, that is pretty much the danger that markets have to navigate through today. It is not just another hot inflation number to worry about but perhaps a combination of data that could leave the Fed with even fewer options in tinkering with monetary policy.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold whipsaws after US CPI as data falls short of bringing an October rate hike back into play
item.description:
Gold nearly fell to new monthly lows yesterday following the higher than expected Core CPI but eventually recovered all the losses. I think the initial reaction was an overreaction, as I mentioned that an uptick to 0.3% wouldn’t have been enough to make the market to fully price in an October rate hike.

In fact, after the knee-jerk reaction, the probability of a rate hike at the upcoming meeting stabilised around 30%, just 9% higher than the 21% probability seen before the CPI release.

Today, we have US PPI on the agenda, but I don’t see it materially changing rate hike expectations. As a result, we could see a similar market reaction to yesterday’s CPI release, unless PPI surprises to the downside, in which case gold could stage a relief rally.

On the geopolitical front, not much has changed. The Saudi Arabia–Houthi conflict continues, while US–Iran negotiations remain at a stalemate. Meanwhile, oil prices continue to rise amid the ongoing Middle East crisis.

Looking ahead, the focus will remain on developments in the Middle East and the Fed’s policy outlook. A breakthrough in US–Iran negotiations could trigger a strong rally in gold, as traders would scale back rate hike expectations. A Fed that is slow to respond to rising inflation could also support gold if inflation expectations rise faster than nominal yields, pushing real yields lower.

On the downside, a more hawkish Fed or a further escalation in the US–Iran conflict could put additional pressure on the precious metal.

 

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that gold(CFD contract) dropped again yesterday following the higher than expected core CPI but eventually recovered all the losses. We still have the downward trendline that could act as resistance. The sellers will likely lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to position for a drop into the 3,885 level. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to pile in for a rally into the 4,700 level next, with the 4,500 level as the first target.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we can see more clearly the downward spike on the CPI release and then the recovery. From a risk management perspective, the sellers will have a better risk to reward setup around the trendline and the 4,228 resistance to keep targeting new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will need the price to break above the trendline and the resistance to open the door for new highs and target the 4,400 level next.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, we have a minor downward trendline that could act as resistance. The sellers will likely lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep pushing into new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break to extend the pullback into the downward trendline and the 4,228 resistance. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

Today we get the US PPI, the US Retail Sales and the latest US Jobless Claims figures. We do have also Fed Chair Warsh speaking very late in the day in a fireside chat with IMF Managing Director Georgieva. He’s against forward guidance, so he might not say anything worthwhile, but it’s worth watching it.

item.title: European stock market open: Equities under pressure as Wall Street selloff weighs on sentiment
item.description:
• Eurostoxx -0.8%
  • Germany DAX -0.4%
  • France CAC 40 +0.1%
  • UK FTSE +0.1%
  • Spain IBEX +0.2%
  • Italy FTSE MIB -0.5%

It's a mixed start to the day in Europe, though the broader mood is leaning more towards the softer side. German and Italian stocks are struggling the most, even if the likes of France and Spain are managing to hold on to marginal gains.

The more cautious mood we're seeing here is not all too surprising after the beatdown in Wall Street yesterday, with the S&P 500 falling by 1.1% and Nasdaq slumping by 1.9%. The hotter-than-expected US CPI report certainly didn't help, with investors having to reassess the prospect of the Fed keeping interest rates "higher for longer".

Having said that, the bigger concern appears to be the ongoing pressure on tech stocks - especially those tied to the AI boom. The latest fall is now starting to question whether the breadth and the momentum of the resilience in the past few weeks are all starting to fall apart.

The fact that 10-year Treasury yields are now down to 5.10%, their lowest in three weeks, suggest that investors are looking beyond the immediate moves in bond yields.

As such, that creates a bit of an uncomfortable backdrop for European stocks. For now, there is some relief from falling bond yields in general. But with inflation concerns still lingering and Wall Street coming under pressure, investors aren't exactly rushing to take on more risk.

We'll have to see if and how US stocks can hold up later in the day to have a better sense of risk appetite in the second half of this week.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: France inflation rises sharply in September as price pressures add to ECB rate hike dilemma
item.description:
• France September final CPI +3.1% vs +3.0% y/y prelim
  • Prior +2.4%
  • France September final HICP +3.4% vs +3.4% y/y prelim
  • Prior +2.6%
  • France September core CPI +1.5% y/y
  • Prior +1.1%

The final figures for September are out and they're not exactly offering much comfort for the ECB. The annual readings confirm another notable jump in price pressures, adding to the inflation concerns we've been seeing across the euro area lately.

Energy prices remain the biggest culprit, surging 21.3% annually in September compared with 16.7% in August. Once again, that is largely triggered by the ongoing fallout from the Middle East conflict.

That being said, we're also starting to see broader price pressures creeping in elsewhere. Core annual inflation picked up to 1.5% from 1.1% previously, helped by a notable jump in services inflation - which rose to 2.4% from 1.9% previously. While core prices are still keeping below the 2% threshold for now, the direction of travel isn't exactly what policymakers would like to see.

For now, the ECB could still be afforded some room to be patient after having already raised interest rates twice this summer. The question now is whether the recent inflation surge warrants another move sooner rather than later. So, the central bank definitely cannot afford to be complacent either.

If higher energy prices start feeding more evidently into services and wages, then the case for another rate hike in December will only grow stronger.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Macro pulse: Treasury yields may be falling for now, but borrowing costs are still painfully high
item.description:
It's been quite a messy reaction in the bond market after the hotter-than-expected US CPI report yesterday. 10-year Treasury yields briefly pushed above 5.30% on the initial reaction before falling back now to around 5.10%, its lowest in three weeks. That's certainly a welcome change for broader markets, but it doesn't really change things all too much for the US economy.

The fact of the matter is just because borrowing costs are getting a little cheaper doesn't exactly mean that they are actually cheap.

Think about it this way. Just imagine that you're looking to buy a house and the bank offers you a mortgage at 7%. A few weeks later, that rate drops to 6.9%. Sure, that's a better situation on paper. However, does it suddenly make that dream home affordable? Probably not. And that's essentially the crux of the problem for the US economy.

10-year Treasury yields serve as a benchmark for borrowing costs across the economy. That goes from mortgage rates to corporate loans and also other forms of long-term financing. Even if these numbers don't move in lockstep with yields, they are still very much influenced by the swings in the bond market.

When yields start to move higher as they have been in the past few months, the impact of that trickles all the way down the economic ladder.

For businesses, that could mean needing to put expansion plans on hold. If financing costs are rising and eating into profits, that leaves little room to borrow millions in wanting to build a new factory or base of operations. As for households, it could mean needing to delay that home purchase or cutting back on other spending to manage existing debt.

And unless yields fall back lower to levels for businesses and households to feel comfortable again, there is no compelling reason to make different decisions to the examples above.

As such, the bigger risk for the economy isn't necessarily just Treasury yields climbing to fresh highs but how long yields will remain at these elevated levels. In other words, the economy doesn't need another surge in borrowing costs to feel the pain. Just the fact that rates are high enough for long enough i.e. "higher for longer" is already enough to do the damage.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: What are the main events for today?
item.description:
EUROPEAN SESSION

In the European session, the main highlight was the UK GDP data which came out higher than expected. Overall, it didn't change much for the BoE other than strengthening further the case for a rate hike at the upcoming meeting, which was already priced in anyway. Traders are expecting a total of four rate hikes by the end of 2027.

Looking ahead, we don't have much on the agenda other that a couple of low-tier releases like the French final CPI and Eurozone industrial production. The data won't change anything for the ECB, so the market reaction will likely be muted.

As a reminder, the market is pricing in an 82% probability of a pause at the upcoming meeting and then a rate hike in December. By the end of 2027, there are three rate hikes priced in.

AMERICAN SESSION

In the American session, we get the US PPI, the US Retail Sales and the US Jobless Claims figures. The PPI Y/Y is expected at 5.4% vs 5.4% prior, while the M/M measure is seen at 0.6% vs 0.4% prior. The Core PPI Y/Y is expected at 4.4% vs 4.6% prior, while the M/M measure is seen at 0.3% vs 0.2% prior.

The Fed's focus has been on core monthly CPI, and even after the uptick to 0.3%, Fed members did not sound like they want to hike at the upcoming meeting, so I doubt the PPI would change much. The market is now pricing a 32% probability of a rate hike in October, up from 21% before the CPI release.

The US Retail Sales are expected at 0.3% vs 1.2% prior, while the Control Group M/M measure is seen at 0.3% vs 1.4% prior. Retail Sales is a very volatile and coincident indicator, so it rarely changes anything for the markets. There's generally a spike, followed by a reversal. Today, the data is released alongside the PPI and Jobless Claims, so there will be something for everyone to suit the price action.

Initial Claims are expected at 200K vs 197K prior, while Continuing Claims are seen at 1709K vs 1716K prior. The Jobless Claims data hasn't been a big market-moving report because the data just continued to support the stable labour market view.

I feel like the markets are starting to look towards the slowdown in growth but there's been very limited sign of that yet. So, a signficant deterioration in Jobless Claims could trigger notable moves in the markets on a potential "growth scare", although one single release won't be enough to set a trend.

CENTRAL BANK SPEAKERS

  • 06:45 GMT/02:45 ET - BoE's Greene (hawkish - voter)
  • 08:45 GMT/04:45 ET - BoE's Breeden (neutral - voter)
  • 09:00 GMT/05:00 ET - BoC's Rogers (neutral - voter)
  • 20:30 GMT/16:30 ET - Fed's Hammack (hawkish - voter)
This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: FX option expiries for 15 October 10am New York cut
item.description:
There are a couple of key expiry levels to take note of on the day, as highlighted in bold below.

The first is a rather chunky one for EUR/USD at the 1.1250 level, with the strike sitting just less than 40 pips away from the spot price. With the dollar retreating alongside Treasury yields as traders continue to digest the US September CPI report, that might keep this expiry level in play especially if the pair continues to nudge higher in the session ahead.

The near-term chart is also starting to turn with EUR/USD buyers breaking back above both the 100-hour and 200-hour moving averages in trading today, the first time in five weeks. That signifies a more bullish near-term picture but all eyes will be on whether Treasury yields will stick with the retreat or reverse back higher as we look to the second half of the week.

But if price action allows for EUR/USD to move closer to 1.1250, then the expiries could act as a magnet to draw price movements and keep trading action more limited around that level heading into the cut.

Then, there is one for USD/JPY at the 158.00 level - just 5 pips away from the spot price. The expiries could keep price action anchored around the figure level heading into the cut. But as mentioned, dollar pairs at the moment remain highly sensitive to moves in Treasury yields. And in the case of USD/JPY, there's also intervention headlines to be mindful of. All of that could easily outweigh the influence of option expiries.

The other expiry level worth noting is for EUR/GBP at the 0.8480 level, with the strike sitting just 11 pips above the spot price. That could attract some attention if the cross trades higher, although the impact will depend on broader euro and sterling flows for the most part.

item.title: Chart of the day: Gold rebounds as dollar and yields fall, but $4,200 remains a major hurdle
item.description:
Gold took a knock after the hotter-than-expected US CPI report, with the precious metal briefly dipping back below the $4,100 mark yesterday. The drop at the time touched a low just under $4,080 before dip buyers stepped back in to arrest the decline.

It seemed like a relatively straightforward move at first but with the dollar and Treasury yields reversing their respective advance, we are seeing gold also bounce back today. The precious metal is being afforded some breathing room again with price now recovering to $4,140 levels.

That throws the ball back over to the buyers' side of the court. Can they actually turn that into something more meaningful?

Looking at the near-term chart above, there's certainly some encouragement for buyers. The latest rebound once again highlights the willingness to defend the downside, with gold recovering back above $4,100 after the sharp plunge yesterday. Having said that, I would not get too carried away with the bounce we're seeing just yet.

The key hourly moving averages continue to present a challenge, with the confluence of the 100-hour (red line) and 200-hour (blue line) moving averages around $4,150-64 having posed as key near-term resistance points for the precious metal in the past weeks.

Beyond that, the $4,200–20 region remains the bigger obstacle. We've seen multiple attempts to push through this area in recent weeks, only for sellers to repeatedly spoil the party.

Besides that, the daily chart also continues to reinforce the need for caution.

The $4,100-20 region has been an important support area since the end of September, with the 78.6 Fib retracement level at $4,117 also coming into play. Despite yesterday's brief break lower, buyers have managed to keep that broader support area in contention for the most part.

However, that is not to say that the downside pressure has dissipated entirely. Gold is also still trading below its 100-day moving average (red line) of $4,245 and that adds another layer of resistance on top of the already stubborn short-term region around $4,200-20.

For now, it seems that dip buyers have done just enough to prevent a more convincing breakdown after the US CPI report. However, that is still not quite enough to suggest that the tide has turned. Buyers will need to get through $4,200-20 as the first hurdle before making a stronger case for that.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: US stocks might have a bigger problem than just hotter inflation
item.description:
US stocks took a hit yesterday from the hotter-than-expected September CPI report, which saw headline prices jump and core annual inflation also push up to 2.6%. Tech shares were the ones bearing the brunt of the pain and with futures also pointing lower today, it is tempting to pin all the blame on inflation. The simple argument is that the last thing that investors want to see is the Fed reaching for another reason to keep rates "higher for longer".

Having said that, the bond market reaction didn't exactly play to the same tune. Treasury yields spiked higher on the data release but quickly gave it all back and are falling even lower today. 10-year yields are now down to 5.10%, its lowest in three weeks. And yet, stocks seem to be struggling still.

So, what gives?

If higher borrowing costs were supposed to be the main concern for equities, shouldn't the pullback in yields offer some relief instead? Besides, the market pricing for the October Fed meeting hasn't shifted all that much too. Traders are pricing in roughly 29% odds of a rate hike, just a mild step up from around 22% odds yesterday.

While hotter inflation certainly isn't helping with market sentiment, it is not entirely convincing to say that the report yesterday tells the whole story behind the selling.

Let's try to dig a little deeper, shall we? Perhaps the bigger problem is that the broader US stock market hasn't actually been doing all that well for quite some time now, even if price action in the S&P 500 itself hasn't been telling us that.

(h/t @KobeissiLetter)

The chart above shows the 52-week correlation between the equal-weighted S&P 500 and the traditional cap-weighted index, with the figure falling to just roughly 0.67 earlier this week. That marks the lowest reading in the chart's history.  For some perspective, this figure stayed largely between 0.95 and 0.99 for nearly 15 years before the Covid pandemic. So, there's definitely a remarkable divergence happening here in the past few years.

But the question is, what exactly does that signify?

The falling figure suggests that the performance of the biggest companies is now a much less accurate representation of what is happening to the average stock in the index. In other words, the S&P 500 is now becoming so top-heavy i.e. dominated by mega-cap names, that the headline index can easily disguise just how much weakness there is elsewhere in the market.

And if that's not convincing enough, let's take a look at the next chart.

This shows that only about 18% of S&P 500 stocks are trading above their 50-day moving average, while just 27% are holding above their 200-day moving average.

But if you look at it from the other angle, it signifies that more than 80% of the stocks in the index are trading below their short-term trend measure. And nearly three-quarters are below their long-term trend measure. Now, that is hardly a picture of a healthy market underneath the surface.

I'm not saying that this is enough evidence to necessarily point to the fact that a major market correction is coming. But when market participation is already this weak, it doesn't take much for selling pressures to spread - especially if the heavyweight names (mostly big tech I would say) holding up the index start to falter as well.

As such, the hotter inflation numbers yesterday may have given Wall Street another reason to hit the sell button. But perhaps the fact that stocks are continuing to feel the pressure even as Treasury yields come off the boil is more to do with the market already looking quite vulnerable well before the inflation numbers landed.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive Asia-Pacific market news: Treasury rally sinks dollar, lifts gold
item.description:
• RBNZ’s Conway says October rate decision completely open, OCR more likely to rise
  • AUD lower: Australian jobs fall 39,300 in September, unemployment at five-year high of 4.7%
  • BOJ’s Koeda says bank should not be overly cautious about raising rates
  • Gold jumps around $40 as Treasury yields retreat from post-CPI high

  • ICYMI: Citi now expects a December Fed rate hike after hotter September US inflation

  • Oil catch up - price gains as Houthis strike Aramco and Iran flags new tactics against tankers
  • Oil: Private survey of inventory shows a huge headline crude oil draw
  • Barclays sees possible Tesla-SpaceX merger announcement before December

Summary:

  • US Treasuries extended their rebound from post-CPI lows, with 10-year yields 21bp below their spike after Wednesday’s inflation data
  • The US dollar fell broadly and gold rallied around $40, helped by lower yields and a Bloomberg report that China may hold more US debt than official data show
  • Oil dipped after a Reuters report that the US is considering easing sanctions on shadow fleet tankers to cut freight rates and boost Gulf oil flows
  • The Australian dollar was the exception in FX, falling after September employment dropped 39,300 and unemployment held at 4.7%
  • The Fed’s Mary Daly said further rate hikes are more likely than not, but signalled no need to move in October. The BOJ’s Koeda said the bank should not be overly cautious about raising rates
  • The Nikkei fell 3.5% and South Korea’s Kospi extended losses as the tech hardware selloff deepened
  • Barclays said a Tesla and SpaceX merger announcement is possible before December, according to Bloomberg
  • Anthropic’s Q3 revenue rose 45% to $16.8bn, Reuters reported. TSMC results are due, with its call at 0600 GMT

Treasuries lead, dollar and gold follow

US Treasuries extended their recovery during the Asian session, pushing 10-year yields 21 basis points below the high they reached after Wednesday’s hotter-than-expected US inflation data. The bond rally had wide effects across markets. The US dollar weakened against most major currencies, and gold climbed around $40.

Lower yields reduce the cost of holding gold, which pays no interest, and that supported the metal. Sentiment toward Treasuries also drew support from a Bloomberg report that China may be holding more US government debt than official figures show. A sharp rise in Canada’s reported holdings of US securities, to nearly $600 billion, has fuelled speculation that China is holding bonds through custodians outside the United States. The claims are unconfirmed.

Gold-related news from Bolivia had limited direct bearing on prices. The country is replacing a central bank certificate for gold exports with a requirement that exporters show the regulator SENARECOM that at least 80% of proceeds are deposited in local banks, aiming to boost dollar inflows and oversight, Bloomberg reported.

Oil

Oil prices edged lower after a US official told Reuters that Washington is considering easing sanctions on shadow fleet tankers to bring down record freight rates and increase oil flows from the Gulf. High fuel prices are a political risk for the administration ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

Australian dollar falls on jobs data

The Australian dollar was the outlier in currency markets, falling while other major currencies gained against the US dollar. Australian employment unexpectedly fell in September, and the unemployment rate held at a five-year high of 4.7%. That prompted traders to scale back bets on another Reserve Bank of Australia rate hike.

Central banks

San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said further rate increases are more likely than not to be needed, according to a Reuters interview. She said the timing is still being considered and signalled no need to move at the October 27-28 meeting. Her comments followed remarks from Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee on Wednesday and the release of the Fed’s Beige Book.

In Japan, Bank of Japan board member Junko Koeda said the bank should not be overly cautious about raising rates, citing upside risks to prices and accommodative financial conditions. She put the neutral rate considerably above 1%, with the policy rate at around 1.25%. In New Zealand, RBNZ chief economist Paul Conway said the late-October decision is completely open, though the cash rate is still more likely to rise.

Stocks

The selloff in technology hardware stocks deepened in Asia, as chipmakers tracked losses on Wall Street amid concern over further Fed rate increases and the financing of artificial intelligence investment. Japan’s Nikkei fell (more than 4%) ... the more I update the more it falls, down 5% now, led by SoftBank, Advantest, Tokyo Electron. South Korea’s Kospi extended its losses to near 8%. Kosdaq fell too, the 8% decline triggering a 20 minute halt. 

Crypto

Bitcoin dropped briefly under USD81,000 with around US$485m in luquidations reported. 

Company news

Barclays said a merger announcement between Tesla and SpaceX is possible before December, according to Bloomberg. Further detail from the note was not immediately available. Anthropic’s third-quarter revenue rose 45% from the previous quarter to $16.8 billion, according to an investor who attended a pre-IPO meeting, Reuters reported. Revenue was $4.7 billion in the first quarter and $11.6 billion in the second.

Still to come

TSMC is expected to report a 65% rise in third-quarter net profit to NT$746.3 billion, about US$23.4 billion, according to an LSEG SmartEstimate. Any result above NT$706.56 billion would be a record and the company’s 11th straight quarter of profit growth. Its earnings call is at 0600 GMT, which is 5:00pm in Sydney and Melbourne.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: RBNZ’s Conway says October rate decision completely open, OCR more likely to rise
item.description:
Conway’s comments keep a late-October hike live, which should support the New Zealand dollar against currencies where rate expectations are falling, most notably the Australian dollar after Thursday’s weak jobs report. That divergence makes AUD/NZD a natural expression of the gap between a dovish-leaning RBA and a still-hawkish RBNZ. By declining to commit, the RBNZ leaves markets highly sensitive to the next round of New Zealand data, so expect pricing to swing between a hold and a hike before the decision. A firm tightening bias also limits the scope for New Zealand yields to fall much further in the near term.

- The RBNZ wants the market to know a hike is coming, just not necessarily when.

Summary:

  • RBNZ chief economist Conway said the late-October rate decision is “completely open”
  • The bank wants optionality between holding and a 25bp hike
  • The RBNZ still sees the OCR as most likely to rise, but has not decided on timing
  • Recent moves in oil and the NZD have added short-term upward pressure on inflation
  • The bank remains confident inflation will slow to its 1% to 3% target band next year

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand’s next interest rate decision in late October is “completely open”, chief economist Paul Conway said, while repeating that the central bank still sees the official cash rate as more likely to rise than fall.

Speaking on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok, Conway said the bank wants to keep its options open between holding the rate steady and raising it by 25 basis points. The RBNZ continues to see the next move in the OCR as most likely to be higher, he said, but it has not decided on timing.

Conway said recent moves in oil prices and the New Zealand dollar have added to inflation pressure in the short term. Even so, the bank remains confident that inflation will slow back into its 1% to 3% target band next year.

The comments leave the October decision finely balanced. By describing the meeting as completely open, Conway avoided pre-committing the bank to a hike, while his reaffirmation of a tightening bias makes clear that a cut is not on the table. That gives the RBNZ room to respond to incoming data, including inflation figures, before the announcement.

The RBNZ’s stance stands out against shifts elsewhere in the region. Across the Tasman, softer Australian jobs data on Thursday prompted traders to cut the odds of a November Reserve Bank of Australia hike to around 15%. In the United States, a hotter inflation report has pushed markets to price a strong chance of a Federal Reserve hike in December.

The key question for the late-October meeting is whether short-term price pressures from energy and the currency prove strong enough to justify acting now, or whether the bank’s confidence in inflation returning to target next year allows it to wait a little longer.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ECB’s Santos Pereira says euro zone inflation is not spreading beyond energy
item.description:
The comments support the view that the ECB can hold its nerve on an energy-led price shock, which should limit pressure for tighter policy in the near term and leave the euro without a fresh rate-driven boost. His attribution of higher yields to fiscal issues rather than inflation is notable for bond traders, since it suggests the ECB sees the selloff as a matter for governments rather than for monetary policy. That points to limited appetite to lean against yields through policy. Natural gas is the swing factor, and a cold start to winter would quickly test his relaxed stance and could revive hawkish pricing.

Álvaro Santos Pereira is the governor of the Banco de Portugal, Portugal’s central bank. That makes him a member of the ECB’s Governing Council.

The ECB can live with an energy shock as long as it stays an energy shock, and so far, says Santos Pereira, it has.

Summary:

  • ECB policymaker Alvaro Santos Pereira said euro zone energy-driven inflation is not spreading to other prices
  • The share of goods and services with prices rising more than 3% or 4% has stayed broadly stable over about two years, he said
  • If inflation starts to broaden, central banks will be forced to act
  • A winter like last year’s would create a problem for natural gas prices
  • He said the recent rise in bond yields is more related to fiscal issues

Energy-driven inflation in the euro zone is not spreading to the wider economy, European Central Bank policymaker Alvaro Santos Pereira said, offering a reassuring signal for the bank as it weighs the risk of higher prices.

Speaking at the Bangkok Economic Festival, the Portuguese central bank governor said the good news was that inflation in Europe had not broadened so far. He pointed to the share of goods and services with prices rising by more than 3% or 4%, which he said had stayed broadly stable over roughly the past two years.

Santos Pereira also made clear where the line sits. If inflation does start to broaden, he said, central banks will be forced to act. That suggests the ECB is prepared to look through an energy shock for now, but would respond if price increases began to spread into other categories.

He flagged natural gas as the main risk. A winter like last year’s would create a problem for gas prices, he said, which would feed directly into energy costs for households and businesses. He also said the recent rise in bond yields was more closely tied to fiscal concerns than to the inflation outlook.

The measure he cited is a breadth or diffusion gauge, which tracks how widespread price increases are rather than how fast prices are rising on average. It is gaining attention among central bankers. Bloomberg Economics highlighted a similar measure for the United States this week, showing fewer US consumer price categories running hot in September. Bank of Japan board member Junko Koeda pointed to the more than 70% of Japanese CPI items rising year on year as evidence that inflation there is taking hold.

For the ECB, the readings to watch are the next euro zone inflation figures, the path of natural gas prices as winter approaches, and whether the share of fast-rising prices starts to climb.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: AUD lower: Australian jobs fall 39,300 in September, unemployment at five-year high of 4.7%
item.description:
The report shifts the RBA debate from when the next hike comes to whether it comes at all, with a pause now looking the likelier near-term outcome. That leaves the Australian dollar out of step with the wider market. While gold and major currencies have risen against the US dollar on lower Treasury yields, the Aussie has stayed near its post-data lows, as a narrowing rate outlook at home offsets the broader dollar weakness. Further AUD underperformance is likely on crosses such as AUD/NZD and AUD/JPY if markets keep paring RBA hike bets. The noisy nature of the data means the next release, and the RBA’s revised forecasts in November, will carry extra weight.

-- Australia’s jobs market blinked in September, and with it went most of the market’s appetite for a November RBA hike.

Summary:

  • Employment fell 39,300 in September against expectations of a 20,000 rise. August was revised down to 29,300 from 39,500
  • Full-time jobs rose 34,400, while part-time jobs dropped 73,700, the weakest month in five years
  • Unemployment held at 4.7% (4.72% unrounded), against 4.6% expected. August was revised up to 4.7%
  • Participation fell to 66.8% from 67.1%, against 67.0% expected.
  • Hours worked rose 0.1% and underemployment edged up to 6.3%
  • November RBA hike pricing fell to around 15% from just under 50% earlier this month, with December near 40%
  • Australian three-year yields fell circa 10bp, and the Australian dollar dropped and has stayed near its lows

Australian employment unexpectedly fell in September, while the unemployment rate held at a five-year high of 4.7%, prompting traders to scale back bets on another Reserve Bank of Australia rate hike.

Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday showed employment dropped by 39,300 in the month, well short of forecasts for a gain of around 20,000. August’s increase was revised down to 29,300. The decline was driven entirely by part-time work, which slumped by 73,700, its weakest month in five years, while full-time employment rose by 34,400.

The unemployment rate was steady at 4.7%, above expectations of 4.6%. August’s rate was revised up to 4.7% from 4.6%, although only just: unrounded, the jobless rate was 4.72% in September against 4.65% in August. A sharp drop in the participation rate to 66.8% from 67.1%, below the 67.0% expected, limited the rise in unemployment, as fewer people were looking for work. Hours worked rose 0.1% and underemployment edged up to 6.3%.

The ABS urged caution in interpreting the seasonally adjusted figures, citing ongoing volatility in the data. That volatility comes at an awkward time for the RBA, which relies on the labour figures to judge how tighter policy is affecting the economy. The split between full-time and part-time jobs, and the swing in participation, have both been noisy from month to month.

Even so, the trend is softening. The unemployment rate averaged 4.6% over the quarter, well above the RBA’s forecast, which is likely to force the bank to revise its projections higher at its November meeting. With the RBA operating under a dual mandate of price stability and full employment, a weaker jobs market makes the risks around further tightening more balanced.

Markets moved quickly to reflect that. Pricing for a November RBA rate hike fell and markets no longer favour a hike before the first half of 2027. Australian three-year government bond yields fell circa 10 basis points.

The Australian dollar dropped on the release and has stayed near its lows, standing out against gains in gold and other major currencies as US Treasury yields have fallen.

---

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ’s Koeda says bank should not be overly cautious about raising rates
item.description:
Koeda’s message leans hawkish: by placing the neutral rate considerably above the current 1.25% policy rate and warning against excessive caution, she keeps further BOJ hikes firmly on the table. That should offer the yen some support, particularly against a backdrop where Fed hike expectations have also risen, which narrows the room for the yen to weaken on rate differentials alone. Her observation that the yen has lost some of its safe-haven role is notable for currency traders, since it suggests geopolitical shocks may now hurt the yen through higher oil import costs rather than help it. Japanese government bond yields may also face upward pressure if markets price a faster path toward neutral.

-

Koeda’s message to markets is that 1.25% is not the destination, and the BOJ shouldn’t let caution slow the trip.

Summary:

  • BOJ board member Junko Koeda said the bank should not become overly cautious about raising its policy rate, given considerable upside risks to prices and accommodative financial conditions
  • She said the neutral rate is likely considerably above 1% and could be above 2% on one estimate, while the policy rate stands at around 1.25% after September’s hike
  • Underlying inflation appears to be becoming anchored at around 2%, with more than 70% of the 500-plus CPI items rising year on year
  • She flagged upside price risks from geopolitics, a weaker yen that has been less of a safe haven, and strong AI-related demand
  • Koeda described Japan’s economy as solid overall and stressed continued balance sheet normalisation

Bank of Japan policy board member Junko Koeda said on Thursday that the central bank should not become overly cautious about raising interest rates, pointing to considerable upside risks to prices and financial conditions that remain accommodative.

In a speech to local leaders in Kumamoto, Koeda said the BOJ should adjust its policy rate in a timely manner while keeping in mind the estimated range of the neutral interest rate, the level at which policy neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. She said the neutral rate is likely considerably above 1%, which she described as roughly the bottom of the estimated range, and that one estimate based on potential growth could put it above 2%. The BOJ’s own estimates imply a nominal neutral rate of around 1.1% to 2.5%. Following the BOJ’s rate hike in September, the overnight call rate stands at around 1.25%, leaving room for further increases on her reasoning.

Koeda said underlying inflation appears to be becoming anchored at around 2%, in line with the BOJ’s price stability target. More than 70% of the over 500 items in Japan’s consumer price index are rising year on year, and the distribution of price changes has shifted higher, she said. With wages also increasing steadily, sustained inflation appears to be taking hold more than before.

She highlighted several sources of upside risk to prices. Geopolitical shocks, including the situation in the Middle East since the spring, have repeatedly driven up crude oil and commodity prices. Koeda also noted that the yen has been less reliable as a safe haven in recent crises, continuing to weaken during this year’s Middle East escalation as oil surged, which has pushed up import costs. Strong global demand linked to artificial intelligence is adding further inflationary pressure.

On the economy, Koeda described recent indicators as solid overall, citing high corporate profits, moderate growth in business investment and continued wage gains. She said rising rates were not expected to significantly reduce household consumption, and that firms’ funding conditions remained favourable.

Koeda also stressed the need to keep normalising the BOJ’s balance sheet, saying its substantial size should not be underestimated. The BOJ is reducing its monthly government bond purchases in stages and plans to hold them at about 2 trillion yen a month from April 2027.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold jumps around $40 as Treasury yields retreat from post-CPI high
item.description:
The rebound suggests markets may have overreacted to the CPI print, with the post-data selloff in Treasuries now looking stretched. For gold, the key level is less a price than a relationship: as long as 10-year yields keep drifting lower, bullion has a tailwind, but the metal remains exposed to any revival in Fed hike pricing. A weaker US dollar alongside lower yields would strengthen the move, so the dollar index is worth watching as confirmation. The US session will show whether the rally has follow-through.

--- Gold and Treasuries are rallying on the same idea: China may not be dumping US debt after all, just keeping it somewhere else.

Summary:

  • Gold has climbed around $40 during the Asian session
  • 10-year Treasury yields are more than 20bp below their high after Wednesday’s hotter-than-expected CPI data
  • A Bloomberg report suggests China may be holding US debt through non-US custodians, inflating Canada’s holdings to nearly $600 billion
  • If confirmed, that would mean foreign demand for Treasuries is steadier than official data suggest, supporting bonds
  • Lower yields reduce the opportunity cost of holding gold, helping the metal recover
  • Iran war and AI-debt worries are also likely adding to safe-haven demand

Gold has climbed around $40 during the Asian session, while yields on 10-year US Treasuries have fallen more than 20 basis points from the high they reached after Wednesday’s hotter-than-expected US inflation data. The two moves appear closely linked, and a Bloomberg report on China’s possible hidden holdings of US debt looks to be adding fuel to both.

The yield spike came after September’s Consumer Price Index showed headline inflation at 3.7% and core at 2.6%, both slightly above forecasts, prompting Citi to call for a Federal Reserve rate hike in December. Since that high, Treasuries have recovered much of the lost ground.

Part of the support appears to come from a Bloomberg report that Canada’s holdings of US debt securities have surged to nearly $600 billion despite a tariff war with Washington. Some investors suspect China is behind the increase, moving US securities to custodian banks outside the United States and masking its true role in financing US deficits. The claims are unconfirmed.

The read-across for bonds is straightforward. China’s officially reported Treasury holdings have been falling, feeding concern that one of the biggest foreign buyers was stepping back just as US borrowing is heavy. If China is instead shifting where it holds its bonds rather than selling them, foreign demand for Treasuries may be steadier than the headline data suggest. That eases one of the worries that had been pushing yields higher.

Gold is benefiting from the same move. Bullion pays no interest, so lower Treasury yields reduce the return investors give up by holding it, and the metal tends to rise when yields fall. The pullback in yields from their post-CPI high has therefore given gold room to recover.

The China report is unlikely to be the only factor. Rising geopolitical stresses involving Iran and unease over heavy borrowing by AI infrastructure companies have also encouraged demand for safe assets ... al;though this has not been much of a factor during Trump's war so far. The link between yields and gold looks the clearest driver, though, so the next test is whether yields can hold their decline. A renewed rise in Treasury yields, perhaps on firmer Fed hike expectations, would likely put gold back under pressure.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Talk grows that China is routing US Treasury holdings through Canada: Bloomberg
item.description:
If China’s holdings are more stable than reported, one of the market’s recurring worries, a steady Chinese exit from Treasuries, would carry less weight, which could ease some concern about foreign demand at US debt auctions. The theory also shows why headline foreign holdings data can mislead traders who read monthly declines as outright selling. Watch auction metrics such as indirect bidder demand, a common proxy for foreign buyers, alongside the custody data, since a mismatch between the two would add weight to the theory. Any official denial or confirmation would be the main catalyst, and neither looks imminent.

---

China’s Treasury holdings may not be shrinking at all, just changing address, and the clue is a $600 billion pile with Canada’s name on it.

Summary:

  • Canada’s holdings of US debt securities have grown to nearly $600 billion of Treasuries and bonds despite a tariff war, Bloomberg reported
  • DoubleLine’s Vitaliy Liberman flagged the rise and was told the growth was actually due to China
  • China is said to be moving US securities to non-US custodian banks in other countries, masking its role in financing US deficits
  • China’s reported Treasury holdings have fallen, but some investors and analysts believe it is shifting holdings rather than reducing them
  • The claims are unconfirmed

Speculation is growing that China may be holding more US government debt than official figures show, after a sharp rise in Canada’s reported holdings of US securities drew attention from bond investors, Bloomberg reported.

According to the report, DoubleLine’s Vitaliy Liberman noticed that Canada’s stockpile of US debt securities had grown aggressively to nearly $600 billion of Treasuries and bonds, despite a tit-for-tat tariff war between the two countries. Liberman was told that the increase was in fact due to China, which has been moving US securities to custodian banks outside the United States. That would mask China’s true role in financing America’s budget deficits.

China’s reported ownership of US Treasuries has fallen. Some investors and analysts believe that decline reflects China shifting its holdings to accounts in other countries, rather than actually reducing them, in order to give the appearance of decoupling from the United States, Bloomberg said. The claims have not been confirmed, and the report summary did not cite official comment from Beijing or Ottawa.

The theory rests on how the data are compiled. US Treasury figures on foreign holdings generally record securities by the country where they are held in custody, not by the ultimate owner. Bonds owned by one country but kept with a bank or clearing house in another can therefore show up under the second country’s name. Analysts have long cautioned that this makes it hard to pin down any single country’s true position, particularly for large official holders.

The question matters because China has historically been one of the biggest foreign buyers of US government debt. A genuine Chinese retreat would remove an important source of demand for Treasuries at a time of heavy US borrowing, while hidden holdings would suggest that demand is more stable than the headline numbers imply. The appearance of decoupling would also carry political weight amid trade tensions.

Investors will be watching the next monthly releases of US Treasury data on foreign holdings for further unusual moves in custodial centres, and for any comment from Chinese or Canadian officials. Without confirmation, the figures point to a plausible explanation rather than an established fact. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bolivia overhauls gold export rules to draw in dollars and lift bank deposits
item.description:
This is a domestic foreign exchange measure rather than a gold price story, so the effect on global bullion markets is likely to be negligible. For Bolivia, a steadier flow of dollars into local banks would ease pressure on the exchange rate and on importers that need hard currency, which supports the recent shift to a flexible rate. The 80% repatriation rule could, however, push some exporters back towards informal channels if they see it as too restrictive, which would undercut the goal. Investors in Bolivian dollar debt are likely to watch for any pickup in reserves and deposit data as a sign the policy is working.

---

Short of dollars, Bolivia is swapping central bank paperwork for a simple rule on gold exports: bring most of the money home.

Summary:

  • Bolivia is overhauling gold export rules to boost US dollar inflows and dollar deposits at domestic banks, Bloomberg reported
  • Exporters must prove to the regulator SENARECOM that at least 80% of export proceeds are deposited in Bolivian financial institutions
  • The central bank-issued certificate needed to ship gold is being scrapped, ending a three-year regime
  • The reform, backed by the president, aims to increase foreign exchange inflows, improve dollar availability and tighten oversight
  • Gold exports reached about $1.02 billion in the first five months of 2026, close to the full-year 2025 total, according to national statistics data

Bolivia is overhauling its gold export rules in a bid to draw more US dollars into the country and lift dollar deposits at domestic banks, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday.

Under the new framework, gold exporters will have to show the mining and metals trade regulator, SENARECOM, that at least 80% of their export proceeds have been deposited with Bolivian financial institutions. In return, they will no longer need a certificate issued by the central bank before shipping gold, ending a certification regime that has been in place for three years. The reform has the backing of the president and is designed to increase foreign exchange inflows, improve the availability of dollars and tighten oversight of the gold trade, according to the report.

The change targets a long-running problem. Bolivia has been short of dollars, and gold has become one of its most important sources of export earnings. Gold exports reached about $1.02 billion in the first five months of this year, according to national statistics data reported by local newspaper Correo del Sur. That is close to the roughly $1.19 billion recorded for the whole of 2025 and well above a slump to around $693 million in 2024.

That slump followed a 2023 gold law that required gold to be sold to the state. Bolivia’s mining minister has blamed the law for pushing trade into contraband channels and has said the framework needs to be improved. The country also recently moved to a flexible exchange rate, ending about three years of a gap between official and parallel rates, which the minister has credited with supporting gold flows.

The new approach effectively swaps central bank control of shipments for a requirement to bring the dollars home. Its success is likely to depend on enforcement. Cooperatives account for almost all of Bolivia’s gold output, and critics, including a former minister, have questioned whether SENARECOM has the capacity to track all the gold moving through the country. The next signs to watch are the volume of gold exports in coming months and whether dollar deposits at Bolivian banks begin to rise.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US weighs easing shadow fleet sanctions to cut record tanker freight rates
item.description:
For oil traders, the signal matters more than the mechanics: Washington is clearly prioritising lower fuel costs ahead of the midterms and is willing to bend sanctions policy to get there. Any added tanker capacity in the Gulf would most directly help Middle East barrels reach Asian buyers, which could narrow the premium Asian refiners pay for alternative supply. Tanker equities, which have benefited from record rates, may be sensitive to headlines like this even if the real capacity added proves small. The political backlash over the Russian diesel waiver suggests any formal move will face resistance from Congress and European allies, so the policy may be slow to take shape.

---

Earlier:

  • Iran’s IRGC orders evacuation of military bases as US strike fears grow: reports
  • Oil catch up - price gains as Houthis strike Aramco and Iran flags new tactics against tankers

--- Washington wants cheaper shipping before the midterms, but the old tankers it is eyeing may not move the needle on freight rates.

Summary:

  • The Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on shadow fleet tankers to cut record freight rates, a US official told Reuters
  • The plan would allow non-sanctioned “legal oil” on previously sanctioned vessels, with companies applying to the Treasury, and aims to move more oil out of the Gulf
  • Energy Secretary Chris Wright referred to the talks in a video message to the World Petroleum Congress, according to Energy Aspects
  • The move follows Trump’s temporary lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel until April 7, which drew criticism from Ukraine, Europe and some Republican senators
  • Energy Aspects said the impact on freight rates would be small, though a few more tankers could become available for Strait of Hormuz runs
  • Industry sources said EU and UK rules binding ship insurers would limit any broad easing

The Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on so-called shadow fleet tankers in an effort to bring down record-high global freight rates, a US official told Reuters on Wednesday.

The shadow fleet refers to vessels that have carried oil and fuel from sanctioned countries, including Russia, Iran and Venezuela, often outside mainstream shipping and insurance channels. According to the official, the discussions centre on allowing “legal oil” to move on previously sanctioned ships. That means crude or refined products not subject to US sanctions, rather than Russian or Iranian oil, which remain under punitive measures. The aim is to get more crude and refined products out of the Gulf, the official said, and companies wanting to use the vessels would need to apply to the US Treasury.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh this week, in a video message, that the administration was discussing the move to tackle freight costs that have hurt demand for US crude, according to research group Energy Aspects. Reuters said it could not obtain the full video or a transcript. The Department of Energy said any easing would not help Russia move oil or oil products, while the Treasury referred questions to the energy department. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The talks come days after President Donald Trump temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel until April 7. That step drew sharp criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, European governments and some Republican senators, who said it would give Russia more revenue to fund its war in Ukraine. Reuters noted that Trump’s push to get Russian diesel onto global markets quickly could add pressure to allow shipments on the vessels.

Tanker rates have climbed to records as the wars in Iran and Ukraine fuel inflation and price US crude out of reach for Asian refiners, pushing them towards Middle East and Latin American supply. High fuel prices are also a political risk for Trump ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

The practical impact may be limited. Energy Aspects said easing the sanctions would do little for freight rates, since most of the ageing tankers involved have already been trading in recent months, though it could free a small number of ships for shuttle runs through the Strait of Hormuz. Maritime industry sources told Reuters that ship insurers would still be bound by EU and UK rules, which would limit any broad easing in rates. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Iran’s IRGC orders evacuation of military bases as US strike fears grow: reports
item.description:
Unconfirmed geopolitical headlines like this often trigger a quick knee-jerk move, followed by a pullback if no confirmation follows, so early price action may overstate the real risk. Traders are likely to add some protection against escalation in the meantime, which tends to show up in safe havens such as gold, the Japanese yen and the Swiss franc. The bigger move would come from any official confirmation or a statement from Washington, since either would turn a rumour into a tradeable event. Positioning ahead of the weekend could also amplify moves if the reports aren’t resolved during the week.

---

Earlier:

  • Oil catch up - price gains as Houthis strike Aramco and Iran flags new tactics against tankers

---

If the reports hold up, Tehran is no longer treating the threat of a US strike as rhetoric, and oil traders will price that in fast.

Summary:

  • Iran’s IRGC has ordered evacuations at a number of military bases across the country, according to initial, unconfirmed reports
  • Iranian officials reportedly told regional diplomats this week that a new US attack is imminent and that they are certain it will happen
  • Neither report has been independently verified, and there is no official statement from Tehran or Washington
  • Oil is the main market channel, given Iran’s role as a producer and its position on the Strait of Hormuz

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has issued evacuation orders for a number of military bases across the country, according to initial reports that have not yet been confirmed.

The reports follow accounts that Iranian officials told regional diplomats this week that they expect a new US attack imminently. The officials reportedly said they were “100% certain” a strike would take place. Neither the evacuation orders nor the officials’ comments have been independently verified, and there has been no official statement from Tehran or Washington on either.

If confirmed, evacuating bases would be a defensive step, typically taken to reduce personnel and equipment losses ahead of an expected strike. It would also suggest Iran’s leadership is treating the threat as real rather than as rhetoric.

For financial markets, the main channel is oil. Iran is a significant oil producer and sits on the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which a large share of the world’s seaborne crude passes. Any escalation that threatens production or shipping in the region tends to lift crude prices quickly, as traders add a risk premium to cover the chance of supply disruption.

The key signals to watch are whether official sources confirm the evacuation orders, any statement from the US administration or the Pentagon, and moves in Brent and WTI crude futures and in safe-haven assets such as gold. Until confirmation arrives, the reports point to rising risk rather than an established development. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
